title: Global Factory Output Hits Four-Year High as AI Demand Lifts Manufacturing PMIs Worldwide
excerpt: September PMI data shows the broadest industrial expansion since early 2022, led by euro zone factories and Asia's chip-exporting economies.
body:
• The Global Manufacturing PMI reached 53.0 in September, its highest level since February 2022, signaling the broadest expansion in industrial output in over four years.
  • The euro zone manufacturing PMI rose to 52.9, its strongest expansion since May 2022, with the output index at a four-year high.
  • Across Asia, South Korea's PMI climbed to 53.9 with export demand growing at its fastest pace in 15.5 years, Taiwan hit 56.7, and Japan's new export orders rose for a ninth straight month.
  • The driver is AI infrastructure spending — semiconductors, servers, capital equipment and data-center components — though rising energy and input costs remain a threat to the recovery.

Global factory activity gained momentum in September as surging investment in artificial-intelligence infrastructure lifted demand for semiconductors, machinery and capital equipment across Europe and Asia. The Global Manufacturing PMI reached 53.0, its highest reading since February 2022, marking a broader expansion in industrial production and new orders after years of stop-start recovery.

The improvement was led by Europe and the AI supply chains of Asia. The S&P Global Eurozone Manufacturing PMI rose to 52.9 in September from 52.7 in August — its strongest expansion since May 2022 — with the output index climbing to its highest level in more than four years. Across Asia, private surveys released Thursday showed factory activity returning to growth in South Korea, Taiwan, Japan and China on solid demand for chips and AI-related goods.

South Korea and Taiwan lead the AI surge

South Korea recorded the sharpest acceleration. Its manufacturing PMI rose to 53.9 in September from 52.3 in August, the highest since May, staying above the 50 mark that separates expansion from contraction for a 10th consecutive month. Export demand grew at its fastest pace in 15.5 years, new export orders posted their biggest jump since March 2011 — with particular strength in Europe and Asia — and manufacturers' optimism for the year ahead improved to an eight-month high, according to Reuters.

"Both new orders and production growth hit the highest for around five-and-a-half years, with anecdotal evidence often linking the expansions to the combined strength of the semiconductor and automotive sectors."

— Usamah Bhatti, economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence

Taiwan, reaping the benefits of the global AI boom, saw its PMI climb to 56.7 from 54.7. Japan's PMI eased to 54.1 from 54.9 — the weakest pace of expansion in six months — but new export orders rose for a ninth straight month on robust demand from Asia and improved sales to the United States. China also expanded last month as easing weather disruptions allowed factories to resume operations.

Capital spending, not consumers, is the engine

The distinguishing feature of this expansion is what is driving it. Companies worldwide are spending heavily on AI data centers, specialized processors, networking equipment, power systems and the other infrastructure needed to run increasingly powerful AI models. That spending cascades into orders for the manufacturers that supply the equipment and components — semiconductors, servers, capital goods and precision machinery.

The effect is most visible in economies with deep industrial and semiconductor supply chains: South Korea, Taiwan, and the euro zone, where Germany's machine-tool and capital-goods sectors benefit directly from investment booms. It is an investment-led cycle rather than a consumer-led one — factories are busier because companies are building capacity, not because households are buying more.

The recovery remains uneven. Indonesia and Vietnam saw activity expand, while the Philippines and Malaysia contracted, the surveys showed. And the euro zone's return to strong growth is notable precisely because its manufacturing sector spent much of 2023 and 2024 in contraction.

The cost pressure cloud

Rising costs are the main risk to the expansion. A renewed rise in energy prices — linked in part to the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran — is clouding the outlook and squeezing manufacturers' margins. In Japan, firms raised selling prices at one of the sharpest rates since late 2022 to pass through input costs. Higher energy and raw-material expenses are raising production costs across the region even as order books fill.

If input costs keep rising faster than selling prices, the PMI gains could translate into thinner margins rather than stronger profits — the classic late-cycle squeeze that has choked off industrial recoveries before.

What to watch

The key question is durability: whether AI capital spending continues at its current pace into 2027, or whether it is front-loaded and set to fade. For investors, the industrial and semiconductor earnings season will show whether the PMI optimism is reaching bottom lines. For policymakers, the tension is between welcoming the manufacturing revival and managing the energy-driven cost pressures that threaten it. The next round of PMI prints — and October's energy prices — will determine whether September marked the start of a sustained industrial upswing or a high point.
